Industry News: Flowtica Verso vs. Comulytic Note Pro: This one wins on speed – and price

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We primarily interact with AI via our phones and computers, but there’s a growing subset of devices that act as a go-between.
  • Also: The Flowtica Verso AI notetaker is my new favorite MagSafe gadget.
  • In a recent development, the Verso is a standalone device, but it also has a MagSafe connector so you can attach it to the back of your smartphone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We primarily interact with AI via our phones and computers, but there’s a growing subset of devices that act as a go-between. The new Flowtica Verso is one such device. And it’s got something that’s new to this class of device — a big touchscreen display.

Also: The Flowtica Verso AI notetaker is my new favorite MagSafe gadget.

In a recent development, the Verso is a standalone device, but it also has a MagSafe connector so you can attach it to the back of your smartphone. Yes, that means yet another screen, which can be a lot to ask. I recently tested the Verso to see if it does what it claims, and compared it to Comulytic’s Note Pro, a device I reviewed favorably earlier this year.

I’m old enough to have been taught a bunch of now obsolete skills, shorthand being one. Another skill that’s come and gone is dictation and transcription. I owned several recorders over the years — from tape to digital — and used them extensively.

I use them, however, because a close encounter with a disease-ridden Scottish tick left me with a bit of cramping and neuropathy in my hands, ultimately nudging me toward investigating more non-keyboard options for my phone.

It has been revealed that aside from being potential time-savers, AI voice recorders are a next-generation accessibility solution. After all, we’re all one misfortune away from needing something to make the digital world more accessible.

According to recent reports, I’ve tried quite a few AI voice recorders, and to date my favorite has been the Comulytic Note Pro, which doesn’t have the Verso’s substantial e-paper display and at the moment costs $130. I’ve used this more than I thought I would, but I have to admit that it still hasn’t integrated itself into my workflow in a way that makes it a must-have.

Also: I cloned my voice with free AI tools – and tested a scam call on my family.

Now that I’ve used both for a while, I think I can offer some grist for the mill for anyone on the fence about whether they want an AI voice recorder with or without an e-paper touchscreen.

Both the Flowtica Verso and Comulytic’s Note Pro are excellent. Despite the Verso having twice as many microphones as the Note Pro (four compared to two, plus a dedicated conduction mic for recording phone calls), I really can’t find a significant difference in recording quality between the two.

The Comulytic Note Pro is smaller, thinner, and lighter, and feels more like a finder card than a recorder. There’s a button to start recording and a tiny 0.8-inch LCD status display to keep you in the loop. And it offers a quite decent battery life of 45 hours (and 107 days on standby). The Note Pro is simple; all you need to worry about is keeping it charged and pressing the button to start recording.

It has been revealed that I want to like the Verso. It’s a nice bit of hardware with a premium, durable feel, and it comes packed with the promise of making my life easier. And some aspects of the device work well. Its voice pickup — even when multiple people are talking — is unnervingly accurate, and the transcription is excellent.

Also: My 3 favorite AI tools for voice dictation while vibe coding.

It has been revealed that it’s also very good at recording phone conversations, though I noticed that using a phone case can reduce accuracy. I’m assuming that this gives the conduction mic, which uses vibration to pick up the other side of phone conversations, less to go on. Battery life is excellent as well, and I have no problem believing Flowtica’s 70-hour runtime claim.

According to recent reports, the Verso is slow. Really, painfully slow.

It has been revealed that with the Note Pro, you press a button, and off you go. With the Verso, there’s a noticeable lag as you sit there waiting for the screen to refresh and the action to kick off.

Also: 5 ways I use ChatGPT Work to save time and money.

E-paper always has a lag, but this goes beyond that. I first found out how frustrating this lag was when I needed to enter a 16-character Wi-Fi passcode. Switching from uppercase to lowercase was tedious, and the delay when switching the keyboard to numeric mode made me think it wasn’t working properly. It was; I just wasn’t giving it time before jabbing some more.

Sources indicate that this lag also reduced my ability to read transcriptions on the device. It was quicker, easier, and less frustrating to look at them on my iPhone because using the Verso’s display felt like going back to an old Kindle Paperwhite (in a bad way).

This slowness never got better, and I never got used to it. As a result, it undermines the usefulness of the touchscreen as both a display and a user input method. This is a shame because it’s a really neat feature that might keep me off my phone more, but that half-second delay between tap and reaction was too much for me. That’s the way of it with devices that have to be power-efficient. Processing power is always the first thing to be sacrificed.

Also: I’ve owned 50+ power stations – one number matters most.

In a recent development, bottom line: I found myself getting frustrated by how slow the Verso was, especially when tapping the screen or pressing the buttons. It all felt too hit-and-miss. The Note Pro might have been just as slow behind the scenes, but there was no display to give me that feedback. Also, everything was done either with a button press or through the app. And since I’ve always got my phone with me, this is no hardship.

According to recent reports, the Verso could also be simplified by removing the “Ask Flowtica” button. I don’t see the point of a separate physical button for a feature I already have on plenty of other devices. And to make things worse, it was painfully slow to use.

Also: 5 USB cables that can fry hardware and steal your data – or worse.

I could whip out my phone, open a browser, and type my question — and quite possibly another two or three — and get an answer while Flowtica was still thinking.

I also received a few “no internet connection” messages with the Verso, and no, my internet connection was fine (I did try it on several Wi-Fi networks, with similar results). Maybe these complications are specific to my device, or maybe they’ll be resolved with future software updates, but these connectivity dropouts certainly got in the way of using the Verso.

Recent findings suggest that the Note Pro just worked. The one button did what it was supposed to do, and there were never any concerns moving recordings from the device to the cloud for transcription.

There’s little point in spending money on an AI voice recorder if you’re not going to use AI to process that raw audio and output it as something useful.

Also: I tried a $200 smartwatch with voice recording – how it beat the Apple Watch.

Both devices come with unlimited transcription, but both companies put limits on how much of the “advanced” features you can use before you have to put skin in the game and buy a subscription. For the Verso, live on-screen transcription, Voice ID, and summaries are advanced features that are limited to 300 minutes a month for those not on a subscription blueprint.

If this feels somewhat confusing — and you’re not alone — the easiest way to think about it is that Comulytic’s free tier includes unlimited basic summaries, while Verso’s main screen feature is metered.

It has been revealed that the Flowtica Verso hits the market with a list price of $299. That’s a steep premium to pay for that e-paper display compared to the competition. And it feels even steeper when the lag gets in the way as much as it did.

Recent findings suggest that the Comulytic Note Pro is under $130, which is about as cheap as it gets for a good AI voice recorder. Even the biggest name in the game, the Plaud Note Pro, is only $189.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI model training.

If I didn’t feel like I was fighting the lag on almost everything I did with the Verso, I’d stick with it. But it’s frustrating, and it’s far easier to slip back into old habits. It’s possible future updates will streamline the Verso’s UI, but if you’re someone who finds it hard to wait half a second for something to happen, it could feel frustrating and is the reason why I’m sticking with the Note Pro for now.

Finally, be aware that subscriptions come into play on both devices, and that the Verso’s screen offers metered free usage for what it calls “AI minutes” before requiring a monthly payment.

#16174. Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (704 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that meta’s executives are rethinking the tech giant’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
  • It has been revealed that the firm’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta.
  • “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that meta’s executives are rethinking the tech giant’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Significant Tech competitor racing to build fresh AI data centers.

It has been revealed that the firm’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”.

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

In a recent development, but all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the organization’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and Upcoming Hampshire. The manufacturer attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

Industry observers note that for comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Significant Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Industry observers note that meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

In a recent development, still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”.

It would very much be in the public interest for other Massive Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

#16173. Google rolls out newly introduced search homepage with AI chat history and no search button

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (414 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Google rolls out newly introduced search homepage with AI chat history and no search button

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (414 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed.
  • Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test.
  • In a recent development, the search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

In a recent development, the search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

The other massive change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s fresh AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

It has been revealed that this change states more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

#16127. Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate

📅 08 Jun 2017 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (102 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Learning to cooperate, compete, and communicate

📅 08 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 1 min read (102 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Multiagent environments where agents compete for resources are stepping stones on the path to AGI. Multiagent environments have two useful properties: first, there is a natural curriculum—the difficulty of the environment is determined by the skill of your competitors (and if you’re competing against clones of yourself, the environment exactly matches your skill level). Second, a multiagent environment has no stable equilibrium: no matter how smart an agent is, there’s always pressure to get smarter. These environments have a very different feel from traditional environments, and it’ll take a lot more research before we become good at them.

📖 0% read

Sources indicate that our Dota 2 result reveals that self-play can catapult the performance of machine learning systems from far below human level to superhuman, given sufficient compute. In the span of a month, our system went from barely matching a high-ranked player to beating the top pros and has continued to improve since then. Supervised deep learning systems can only be as good as their training datasets, but in self-play systems, the available data improves automatically as the agent gets better.

#16091. Industry News: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm

Industry News: Reptile: A scalable meta-learning algorithm

📅 07 Mar 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (91 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that we’ve developed a simple meta-learning algorithm called Reptile which works by repeatedly sampling a task, performing stochastic gradient descent on it, and updating the initial parameters towards the final parameters learned on that task. Reptile is the application of the Shortest Descent algorithm to the meta-learning setting, and is mathematically similar to first-order MAML (which is a version of the well-known MAML algorithm) that only needs black-box access to an optimizer such as SGD or Adam, with similar computational efficiency and performance.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’re releasing an analysis showing that since 2012, the amount of compute used in the largest AI training runs has been increasing exponentially with a 3.4-month doubling time (by comparison, Moore’s Law had a 2-year doubling period)[^footnote-correction]. Since 2012, this metric has grown by more than 300,000x (a 2-year doubling period would yield only a 7x increase). Improvements in compute have been a key component of AI progress, so as long as this trend continues, it’s worth preparing for the implications of systems far outside today’s capabilities.

Industry observers note that we’ve trained an agent to achieve a high score of 74,500 on Montezuma’s Revenge from a single human demonstration, better than any previously published result. How AI training scales

📅 14 Dec 2018 | ⏱️ 1 min read (84 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that we’ve discovered that the gradient noise scale, a simple statistical metric, predicts the parallelizability of neural network training on a wide range of tasks. Since complex tasks tend to have noisier gradients, increasingly large batch sizes are likely to become useful in the future, removing one potential limit to further growth of AI systems. More broadly, these results show that neural network training need not be considered a mysterious art, but can be rigorized and systematized.

📖 0% read

We’ve created MuseNet, a deep neural network that can generate 4-minute musical compositions with 10 different instruments, and can combine styles from country to Mozart to the Beatles. MuseNet was not explicitly programmed with our understanding of music, but instead discovered patterns of harmony, rhythm, and style by learning to predict the next token in hundreds of thousands of MIDI files. MuseNet uses the same general-purpose unsupervised technology as GPT-2, a large-scale transformer model trained to predict the next token in a sequence, whether audio or text.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Why responsible AI development needs cooperation on safety

📅 10 Jul 2019 | ⏱️ 1 min read (102 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

We’ve written a policy research paper identifying four strategies that can be used today to improve the likelihood of long-term industry cooperation on safety norms in AI: communicating risks and benefits, technical collaboration, increased transparency, and incentivizing standards. Our analysis shows that industry cooperation on safety will be instrumental in ensuring that AI systems are safe and beneficial, but competitive pressures could lead to a collective action problem, potentially causing AI companies to under-invest in safety. We hope these strategies will encourage greater cooperation on the safe development of AI and lead to better global outcomes of AI.
